Officials in Laos are expected to outline the conclusion of their investigation into the mass methanol poisoning incident at the Nana Backpackers Hostel in Vang Vieng in November 2024.

Melbourne teenagers Bianca Jones and Holly Morton-Bowles, both 19, died following the incident.

Their fathers have told the ABC they are "furious" over the proposed charges, calling on Australia to "intervene".

A Melbourne father whose daughter died from methanol poisoning in Laos has said he is "disgusted" over the inadequacy of the charges expected to be laid against the people allegedly responsible.

Melbourne teenagers Bianca Jones and Holly Morton-Bowles, both 19, died after a mass methanol poisoning incident at the Nana Backpackers Hostel in Vang Vieng in November 2024.

Two Danish women, an American man and a British woman also died in the incident.

Officials in Laos are expected to outline the conclusion of their investigation into the incident on Friday afternoon.

The ABC understands that Laos officials could seek to charge those allegedly responsible with two offences that collectively carry up to one year in jail, and a maximum fine of $1,600.

On Friday morning, the Australian government called in Laos's ambassador in Canberra over the matter, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said in a statement.

Shaun Bowles and Mark Jones have expressed disbelief at the proposed charges and penalties, calling on the Australian government to intervene. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

Bianca's father, Mark Jones, told the ABC that "[feeling] furious would be an understatement".

"To think that the lives of my daughter, and another five people, are worth less than a year in prison and less than $1,600," he said.

"I don't have words for the disgust that I have with what the Laos authorities are suggesting is meant to be justice for the deaths of six tourists.

"I'm calling on the Australian government to do all they can to intervene.

"For Prime Minister Albanese to reach out to his counterpart in Laos to insist that some form of genuine justice is served for the deaths of two Australian citizens."

Bianca's mother, Michelle Jones, said the charges expected to be laid showed "their lives didn't even matter".

"We're just really appalled by it all. They were just going over to have a bit of fun and doing the rite of passage that every child or teenager does," she said on ABC News Breakfast.

"So for that outcome, it was just devastating."

The Australian government has been briefed on the charges that could be brought, including operating a business illegally and producing or selling consumer goods that are hazardous to health.

Ms Wong said the government was "deeply frustrated and bitterly disappointed" that Laos authorities were "not pursuing the most serious charges".

"Since their deaths, Australia has advocated for a thorough and transparent investigation that takes into account all available evidence and for those responsible to be held to account," she said in a statement.

The small town of Vang Vieng in Laos is a popular tourist destination for backpackers. (Reuters: K Yoganand/WWF)

"The Prime Minister and I appointed Mr Pablo Kang as Special Envoy to continue Australia's efforts and explore all avenues to achieve progress in the investigation.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has been contacted for comment.

"We recognise how disappointing and frustrating this development will be," DFAT said in a letter to the teenagers' families.

"Particularly given the efforts that have been made over many months to encourage consideration of the most serious available charges."

The Australian government calls in the Lao ambassador in Canberra, amid criticism of the country's response to a fatal methanol poisoning.

"We will again convey our strong views about the inadequacy of the charges directly to the Lao authorities."

Earlier this year, the Australian government called in the Lao ambassador in Canberra, amid criticism of the country's response to a fatal methanol poisoning.

Holly's father, Shaun Bowles, said it was "very hard to comprehend" the proposed charges and the penalties they carried.

"We've tried every avenue we've had open to us," Mr Bowles said.

Bianca Jones and Holly Morton-Bowles were travelling around South-East Asia, when the fatal mass poisoning event happened.

More than a dozen people fell seriously ill in November 2024 after drinking at the Nana Backpackers Hostel in Vang Vieng.  (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough )

More than a dozen people fell seriously ill in November 2024 after drinking at the hostel.

In January, 10 people linked to the hostel were found guilty of destroying evidence in a Lao court.

They were fined an amount that Mr Bowles and Mr Jones understood to be $185 and given suspended sentences.

Although that charge only related to the death of the US tourist.
